Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to The Theory of Moral Sentiments and files it under Scottish Enlightenment. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Adam Smith

Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish moral philosopher and political economist of the Enlightenment, professor at Glasgow and friend of Hume. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) precedes The Wealth of Nations (1776), which analyzes markets, division of labor, and commercial society.

How to read this passage

Greek distinctions among eros, philia, and agape, Confucian relational ethics, and modern debates about romantic love keep the theme philosophically precise rather than merely sentimental. This passage enters that discussion through love, character.

Concepts in this quote

Love
Love in philosophy ranges from friendship and desire to care, justice, and the transformation of the self.
Character
Character appears in this archive as a live philosophical concern—not a slogan. These verified English passages show how thinkers treat character as a problem of judgment, practice, or explanation.
